findings.where: The full-width blue 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' band with its white Subscribe button, directly under the hero (on desktop it starts at the fold; on phone it sits inside the first scroll)
findings.fault: The page asks for a second, competing action right after the one personal action. It also switches to the third person ('Mark's') straight after his first-person hero, and it offers a briefing series nothing on the page shows exists. The parts map shows Subscribe goes only to #subscribe, and the page has no subscribe section. A visitor who acts on this offer gets nothing. A full-width colour band with a centred slogan and a button is a marketing-funnel pattern any consultancy could use.
findings.who_objects: The founder objects: the brief asks for one message and one action, first person throughout, nothing salesy, and no invented claims. A development-bank officer would object too. They click Subscribe, nothing happens, and the page now reads like a newsletter push rather than a personal adviser they can write to.

findings.where: First screen, header strip (name, divider, logo) and the hero as a whole
findings.fault: The page has no navigation. The brief's first screen calls for a nav, and nothing on the first screen leads to his work, CV, articles or a Contact label. Apart from the email, a first-time visitor has nowhere to go to check who he is.
findings.who_objects: Procurement staff at multilateral banks judge an adviser by his work history and publications before they write. With no route to either, they must take the lede's claim on trust or leave.

findings.where: Hero: the heading, the lede and the area around the action
findings.fault: The first screen claims standing ('I advise multilateral development banks, development agencies and governments') but gives no proof near the action. It names no body that asked for his work, no region or base country, and no recent talk or venue. The 5-second test answers what he does and for whom, but not where, and not why a visitor should believe it.
findings.who_objects: A development-agency visitor needs to be sure he has done this kind of work for bodies like theirs, in their region (first-visit trust items 3 and 6). Here they get an opinion line and an unsupported claim right beside the request to write to him.

findings.where: Hero photograph (desktop right half; phone above the heading), and its repeat in the motion sketch
findings.fault: The 'Mark at work' direction turns into a cut-out head and shoulders keyed onto flat slate. The lectern and event that show him working are gone, so the image reads as a large pasted headshot rather than a man speaking at a named event. At 1440 px the face fills half the screen, which leans towards a campaign poster rather than a quiet advisory presence. (This concerns the candidate's keying and scale, not the stand-in photo itself.)
findings.who_objects: The founder chose v7 to show Mark at work, and a photo at a named event is itself proof (feel the CV). A senior public-sector reader may find the oversized floating face slick or political, the opposite of the refined, unsalesy tone the brief asks for.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture card 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the 'Abundance' Challenge · Lecture · 23 April 2026'
findings.fault: The newest talk is shown with a date but no venue or host body. That leaves out the piece of proof that makes a talk count.
findings.who_objects: A bank officer weighing his standing looks at who invited him to speak. Without the venue, the card is just a title and a date (feel the CV: 'the newest article or talk … with its venue').
